en: The Ritual for the Gaṇacakra.
Oṃ, homage to the venerable Nairātmikā!
Having bowed to the heroic Śrī Heruka, whose very nature is great bliss,
I shall explain the procedure for the gaṇacakra and the bali offering associated with Hevajra.

At night on a festival day, it is praised; likewise, the wheel should be raised every day for seven days, or once a year, with a joyful mind and skillful hands. One should indeed perform it every month thereafter, as often as possible according to one's means.

Furthermore, it is taught that a wheel constructed on a cremation ground, on a riverbank, in a forest, or even in a garden—provided it is not situated in a place overcome by the rains, nor one that causes fear through negligence, nor one that brings obstacles—is fruit-bearing when located in one's own home or similar dwelling. As for the syllables at the tips and the center: [the text continues].
Having attained the glory of the authentic lineage, he turned his face away from worldly dharmas;
he was endowed with the virtues of mindfulness, vigor, compassion, renunciation, ethical discipline, and patience.
Speaking kindly, with a smiling face, and free from greed and deceit—
this is the assembly of the mandala as taught by the Lord Hevajra.
His disciples were great-souled, free from envy, greed, and other such faults;
having received initiation, they were endowed with intelligence, patience, mindfulness, vigor, and compassion;
following the conduct of the samaya, they desired the succession of the elders.
They are virtuous, possessed of moral discipline, and devoted to faith and devotion.
Devoted to the Guru, a knower of the Vajra of Action, impartial toward all, with senses subdued,
endowed with mindfulness, vigor, and compassion, possessed of virtuous qualities and conduct,
he discerns what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, and is free from greed and deceit.
One who is constantly proficient in the secret signs (*cchomā*) and so forth, and who observes the conduct of the pledges (*samaya*),

should thereafter, at the appropriate time, invite the practitioners of the pledges (*samayin*) who are intent upon the meditation on the conduct of the pledge of gnosis (*jñānasamaya*). This should be done by offering flowers, betel, and other such items as they have obtained.
Then, having consecrated the solid food, soft food, as well as what is to be eaten, drunk, sucked,
and licked with the Āṣāḍha vessel, the wise man should establish them with devotion.
The first row is known to face east, extending toward the northwestern direction;
the second faces north, reaching to the edge of the southwestern quarter;
the third faces west, extending toward the northeastern and northwestern corners.
The third [mudrā] is declared by the Buddha to be the destroyer of all Māras;
then, having invited those who have been addressed with devotion, one should summon them into the maṇḍala of the Gaṇa.
Reciting the entry mantra, one should respectfully cause them to enter.
In this regard, the mantra for entry is as follows:
O hero, Sonīla has seized me; O Māṇika, protect my life with your staff and grant me your grace.
I have met [you], O savior from the cycle of existence; I am going.
The yoginī, pure through the service of all auspiciousness, has arrived.

Having entered and prostrated before the Lord of the Gaṇas, those of great majesty should take their seats according to their respective positions, without overstepping the order of seniority based on consecration;
adorned with bone ornaments and the like, they remain joined with their consorts (prajñā) on their left.
There, she was worshipped abundantly with garments, garlands, and other offerings on two occasions.
One should offer food and other items twice as much to the leader of the assembly as to the assembly itself.
The Karmavajrī should present the general offering vessel, filled with bali-oblations and endowed with flowers, incense, and so forth, to another mantra-practitioner.
The practitioner, having performed prostration, should again entreat the guru.

I bow to the circle of the supreme heroic Yoginīs, which is free from all conceptual constructions, possesses an ever-unchanging vision of the equality of existence and peace, and is exultant in the essence of incomparable bliss.
Again, the entreaty:

May all the heroes (*vīra*) and heroines (*vīreśvarī*), headed by the King, attend to me; out of compassion for me for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, and for the purpose of pacification and so forth, having entered into the yoga of their own chosen deity, may they partake [of the offerings] through the ritual of fire-offering (*homavidhi*), preceded by worship and bali-offerings.
Then, the leader of the assembly (gaṇādhyakṣa), having exclaimed "Excellent! Excellent!", should speak thus:
"May you all preside over the vessel and the hand in common.

Then, all [the members], rising from their seats in order of seniority, should bow to the circle together with the Lord of the Assembly (gaṇeśa) and request permission, saying: "Grant us the feet [of the master]."

There, having been authorized by the preceptor, they sit cross-legged on their seats all around; maintaining the yoga of their chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), they take a drop of nectar with the thumb and ring finger, rub their two hands together, place the left hand over the vessel, and perform the transformation of the syllables with the syllable *haṃ* (or *hā*).

Again, having placed [the substance] upon the right hand with the syllable *hoḥ*, one performs the destruction of odor; likewise, having covered both hands with the syllable *hrīḥ*, one performs the destruction of potency and brings about the state of immortality (*amṛtatva*). Then, having taken three drops with the left thumb and forefinger, one produces the syllable *vaṃ* within a triangular mandala through the meditative resolve (*adhimokṣa*) on the Dharmadhātu-mudrā, according to the method of emitting the bodhicitta. Having produced the maṇḍala-circle by way of the relationship between the support and the supported, one worships and praises each [deity] with their respective offering mantras and presents the *bali* offering, concluding with: *hā hoḥ hrīḥ svāhā*.

Having recited this mantra three times, one should sprinkle water on the head, apply a *tilaka* mark on the forehead, and place the mantra upon the tongue; then, becoming the mouth of the mantra, one should present the food offering (*naivedya*) twice—once to the Bhaṭṭāraka in the vessel and once in the *bali*-offering bowl. According to the specific ritual action and the application of colors, one should establish the foundation for the *bali* by this procedure: within the *dharmodayā* produced from the syllable *HŪṂ*, upon a double lotus born from the syllable *PAṂ*, and above a wind-maṇḍala produced from the transformation of a blue syllable *YAṂ*, [there arises] that which is born from a red syllable *RAṂ*.

Above a triple-stranded cord, a flame, the sun, and a circle of fire, upon three severed heads, one should visualize a lotus vessel arising from the syllable *Āḥ*. Within it are the ten pledge-substances, such as beef and so forth, which have ripened from the ten seed-syllables beginning with *Vum*, and which are empowered by those very seeds. Having observed this, one sees a *Hūṃ* born from a moon arising from the syllable *Āṃ*, and above that, a *Vajra* born from *Hūṃ*, empowered by its own seed-syllable. Upon that, one visualizes a white *Hūṃ* in the form of a lid. Through the cooking by the fire fanned by the wind, leaving aside the *Vajra*, all of that melts and comes to rest within the skull-cup.

Then the vajra, having been raised up four or five times, melts and dissolves right there. Thereupon, having gratified the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas residing in infinite and boundless world-systems with rays from the three principles (*tritattva*), one draws forth their nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*) and causes it to enter that very place. One should perceive that nectar as cool, empowered by the three principles. Then, with the mantra *oṃ āḥ jñānāmṛte hūṃ*, the practitioner with vajra in hand should touch the vessel of the offering (*balipātra*).

Thereafter, having meditated upon the three cities of liberation (mokṣapuratraya) in the center, above, and below by means of the three principles (tritattva), adorned with red eight-petaled lotuses, one should summon the ten obstacles (vighnas) beginning with Indra located in the ten directions by means of the ten wrathful kings (krodharāja) flashing forth from the seed-syllable in one's own heart: Having addressed them with: "Oṃ, Indra, Jama, Jala, Jakṣa, Bhūta, Vahni, Vāyu, Rākṣasa, Candra, Sūrya, Mada, Vappa, Tala, Pātāla, Ardha, Sappa, Sāhā," [one should then recite]: "Oṃ Vajragauri, attract [them]! Jaḥ!"

Having drawn them in with "Oṃ vajracauri praveśaya hūṃ," one causes them to enter the three lotuses; then, having bound them in their respective places with the "sphoṭabandha" [seal] using "Oṃ vajravettāli bandhaya vaṃ," and having gratified them with the bell using "Oṃ vajraghasmari paśya ghaṇṭayā toṣaya hoḥ," one should gaze upon them according to their proper positions.

There, on the eastern petal of the center, is Indra, born from the syllable *Iṃ*, yellow in color, thousand-eyed, holding a vajra in his hand, and mounted upon Airāvaṇa. On the southern petal is Yama, born from the seed-syllable *Yaṃ*, with a staff and noose, having a buffalo as his vehicle, and black in color. On the western petal is Varuṇa, born from the seed-syllable *Vaṃ*, white, with a makara as his vehicle, and holding a noose in his hand. In the north is Yakṣa, born from the seed-syllable *Yaṃ*, yellow, with a human as his vehicle, and holding a bilva fruit in his hand. All of these wear every kind of ornament and possess jeweled crowns.

Yama has the sun as his seat and the radiance of the sun. The remaining [deities] have the moon as their seats and the radiance of the moon. In the northeast is Bhūtapati (the Lord of Beings), who is three-eyed, wears a crown of matted hair, and has a bull for his vehicle; he holds a trident in his hand, is white in color, wears a garment of tiger skin, has his body smeared with ashes, is adorned with snakes, has the moon as his seat, and possesses the radiance of the moon.

In the southeastern petal is Vahni, who is Lambodara; he is red and corpulent, rides upon a goat, is clothed in red robes, holds a rosary and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), wears a crown of matted hair, sits upon the sun, and possesses the radiance of the sun. In the southwestern petal is Rākṣasa; he has tawny hair standing erect and loose, holds a dagger and a skull-cup, is wrathful with knitted brows, is black, stands upon a corpse, sits upon the sun, and possesses the radiance of the sun.

On the petal of Vāyu is Vāyu, dark blue, wearing a jewel crown, mounted on a deer, adorned with all ornaments, seated upon the moon, and possessing the radiance of the moon. In the pericarp is the goddess Pṛthivī, yellow, wearing divine garments and all ornaments, holding a water-jar in her hand, possessing the radiance of the moon, and standing encircling the earth; [around her] are masses of hungry ghosts (preta). Indra and the other four [directional guardians] hold a noose made of snake-skin in their left hands. All of them stand in the pratyālīḍha posture.

Furthermore, upon the eight petals of the lotus of the Dharmodaya above: on the eastern petal is Candra, riding a white horse, wearing a jewel crown, holding a water-lily in his hand, adorned with all ornaments, and possessing a radiance equal to himself. On the southern petal is Sūrya, of the color described [above], adorned with all ornaments, wearing a jewel crown, riding a green horse, holding a white lotus with both hands, and possessing a radiance equal to himself. On the western petal is Budha, riding a mouse, seated upon the sun, possessing solar radiance, holding an arrow in his hand, and wearing a jewel crown.

On the northern petal is Śukra, white in color, wearing a jewel crown, holding a spear, seated upon a solar disc, and possessing solar radiance. On the northeastern petal is Maṅgala, with hair tied upward, holding a lotus, red in color, seated upon a solar disc, and possessing solar radiance. On the southeastern petal is Bṛhaspati, yellow, wearing a jewel crown, holding a mace, seated upon a solar disc, and possessing solar radiance. On the southwestern petal is Śanaiścara, black, tawny-eyed, holding a trident, seated upon a solar disc, and possessing solar radiance.

On the petal in the northwest are Rāhu and Ketu, of very dark and smoky color respectively, seated upon sun-disks and possessing the radiance of the sun. Rāhu is intent on the gesture of devouring the wheel of saṃsāra after having drawn it in; Ketu holds his hands in the *sampuṭa-añjali* (clasped-together) mudrā. In the central circle is Brahmā, four-faced and four-armed, holding a triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) and with one hand in the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*). With his remaining two hands he holds a rosary and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). He is yellow in color, has a swan as his vehicle, is stout, short in stature, wears matted hair (*jaṭin*), and is invested with the sacred thread (*yajñopavītī*). He is seated upon the moon and possesses the radiance of the moon.

Having encircled Brahmā, the [deities] of the Brahmakāyika and Brahmapurohita [heavens], as well as the Dūṣita, Śuddha, and Ābhāsvara [heavens], are all to be visualized. Upon the eight petals of the lotus situated at the base of the Dharmodaya, in the sequence of the cardinal and intermediate directions: Vāsuki is yellow; Padma is white; Karkoṭa is red; Takṣaka is black; Śaṅkhapāla is yellow; Mahāpadma is dark blue (śyāma); Ananta is pale white (pāṇḍara); and Kulika is reddish-brown (karndura?).

And those eight [deities] wear jewel crowns, have human faces, and their heads are marked by hoods; they bear all ornaments and are accompanied by asuras and hell-beings. In the pericarp is Śeṣa, white, with a human face and hoods. Having thus stabilized them, one should then transform them into the form of Śrī Heruka through the instruction of a true guru. Those situated above should be visualized as the form of Body by means of the syllable OṂ; those situated below as the form of Speech by means of the syllable ĀḤ; and those in the middle as the form of Akṣobhya by means of the syllable HŪṂ.
Furthermore, they should be meditated upon according to the appropriate application by means of the syllable HŪṂ.

Then, having worshipped with the water for the guest-offering, the water for the feet, and so forth, along with food offerings, flowers, and other items, one should visualize a five-pronged vajra produced from the syllable *hūṃ* in the right hand, and a bell produced from the syllable *āḥ* upon a moon disc in the left hand.

O Adornment! O Void! O Non-perception! O Liberation through Truth! O Liberation through Dharma! You are the Faultless One! You are the Holder of the Body! You are *Hūṃ*! *Ho*! *Ho*! *Ho*! By means of Wisdom and Skillful Means, the resonance consisting of the nature of Wisdom and Skillful Means: *Oṃ vajradharmaraṇata saṃprāraṇata sarvabuddhapracalite prajñāpāramitānādasvabhāvena vajrasattvahṛdayasaṃtoṣaṇi hūṃ phaṭ*.
Thus, preceded by the brandishing of the vajra while ringing the bell,
one should announce the task with the mantra: *yaṃ edaṃ bali bhuñja jighahu lapuyya māsaṃ viṃṭā ahma kajja sarvasāhakhāntikhuṇi teṭa gā yāyaṭada*, and [conclude] with the vajra-mudrā.
Oṃ, the syllable A is the gateway to all phenomena because they are primordially unarisen; oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
One should offer [the oblation] in due order with the mantra: *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *jaḥ*, *hrīḥ*, *hūṃ*, *phaṭ*.

Then the Blessed One, having tasted the nectar through the tube of the rays of his tongue—which were the size of white *hūṃ* syllables, *bhaya* syllables, barley, and fruits—[became] like a blue lotus (*utpaṅga*). Having bestowed the bliss of arising upon the circle of the Goddesses, he became joyful together with the circle.
Having thus meditated and recited the hundred-syllable mantra, preceded by the ringing of the bell:
"O Vajraḍāka, who in every way purifies all the sins of all sentient beings and brings about the awakening to all phenomena— homage be to you!"
Having seen the world overcome by hatred, for the sake of pacifying the world's hatred,
O Jina Vairocana, Lord, O Mohavajra, homage be to you!
Homage to you, the Sage of the Perfections, who, having seen the world as consisting of women, became a yoginī of selflessness; homage be to you, the Seal of Māyā!
Having seen the world overcome by delusion, you who bring about the destruction of all delusion— O Vajrasattva, Great King, Vajra of Hatred, homage be to you!
Seeing the world overcome by pride, you are the foundation for the destruction of all pride;
O Great King Vajrasūrya, Vajra of Passion, homage be to you!
O Great King Hayagrīva, who brings about the destruction of all passion upon seeing the world overcome by passion— homage be to you, the destroyer of slander!
Seeing the world overcome by envy, you who bring about the destruction of all views—
O King of all kings, O Great King, O You of all forms, homage be to you!
Having seen the world overcome by delusion, the Vajrī assumed the form of Gaurī for the sake of pacifying the world's delusion; therefore, O Gaurikā, homage be to you!
Seeing the world overcome by hatred, the Vajra-holder assumed the form of Caurī in order to pacify the world's hatred; therefore, O Caurī, homage be to you!
Seeing the world overcome by pride, the wielder of the thunderbolt assumed the form of Vettālī in order to pacify the pride of the world; therefore, salutations to Vettālī.
Seeing the world overcome by passion, for the sake of accomplishing great passion, the King assumed the form of Ghasmarī; therefore, homage to Ghasmarikā!
Homage, homage! Let there be homage to you who possess the non-dual form of selflessness;
let there be homage to you, Hevajra, who embodies the five wisdoms and the three bodies.
I bow to Śrī Heruka, who is most terrifying with his formidable fangs, adorned with garlands and strings of mantras, and who devours great flesh.

Having praised [the deity] in this way and offered betel, flowers, and so forth, with palms joined and hollowed, he should request the accomplishment of his desired aim and establish an auspicious connection with the king and others.
The goddesses are the authority, the sacred pledge is the authority, and their spoken words are the supreme authority;
by this truth, may they [be successful].
The goddesses are the cause of my grace.
Those whose resolve is unshaken by attachment to existence or its cessation, who perceive all phenomena as being like space in their true nature,
and whose lords of the mind are swollen with the waters of profound compassion;
O goddesses, show me your supreme compassion! Act, act!
Having thus asked for forgiveness with this recitation.
Oṃ! The purpose of all sentient beings has been accomplished for you; having granted [this], go as you wish to the realm of the Buddhas, and return once more.
Muḥ.
Thus, one should dismiss [the deities] by snapping the fingers of the thumb and ring finger on the back of the left hand.
Then, one should offer a bali-oblation at a crossroads.

Furthermore, for the offering of the intermediate *bali*, the *ācārya* and all [the others] should prepare the *balipātra*. Within the fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*) of the Caṇḍālikā fire located inside the *nirmāṇacakra*, using the hand as a vessel, they should satisfy the circle of their chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatācakra*) by means of the internal homa-rite performed with *yava* grains and fruits the size of a *vajra*-tongue produced from the syllable *HŪṂ*. This is done through non-dual yoga (*advayayoga*). The oblations should be offered with the pouring of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Immediately thereafter, one should offer the *bali* according to the ritual. Then the Guru, having drunk from it himself, should give the vessel to him out of his compassionate nature.

One should collect [the water] from the recitation of the verses. Neither too fast nor too slow, having drunk a little and filled [the vessel], one should respectfully present it while reciting the verses; bowing with the joined palms (*añjali*), one should enter again.
Therein is the verse on giving:
Behold the purified Dharma; indeed, there is no distinction based on birth.
The Brahmin, the dog, and the Caṇḍāla are all consumed within a single nature.
Welcome to this priceless Dharma, O King, which has come to you;
it is free from the entanglements of householders and is praised by those who know the truth.
One should not fill the vessel to the very brim, nor should one dry it out completely;
one should not give anything by oneself, nor should one pour honey upon the ground.
And one should not give food or drink to one another without permission;
nor should one who is hungry take food or drink on his own initiative.
But the Karmavajrī, taking the drink and so forth herself, incurs no fault;
there, the practitioners pay homage to her again and again.
He who causes the bowl to fall to the ground, or gives it to another,
or from whose hand it falls, is to be disciplined by the leaders of the community.
If one does not dry it oneself.
One should avoid arrogance, excessive hatred, sloth, improper talk,
dispute, quarrel, anxiety, and despondency;
one should abandon the practice of what is forbidden, which is a gross and great fault rooted in the very foundation.
The emergence from an offense is proclaimed to be accomplished according to the prescribed rule.
Those who are addicted to women and liquor, those who are perfumed with *sihlaka*, and those who are negligent—
entry [into the monastery] must not be granted to them if one desires the welfare of the Teaching.
If one who is ignorant of the ritual rules and advanced in years should be of a foolish nature,
then one should provide him with food, drink, and other sustenance in another location;
even his eating should be done in another form by one whose mind is corrupted by ignorance.
Therefore, the wise who desire success for the sake of accomplishment should not remain [in ignorance];
they should speak of the intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣa*), the great secrets, the extensive conventions of the commitments (*samaya-saṃketa*),
and other well-spoken, heart-pleasing words that are pleasing to themselves.
Having attained momentum, [the practitioner], being joyful and having gone outside,
should himself take the remains and offer the *bali* facing the threshold;
then he should exit with this mantra to be recited hereafter.
With its essence vibrating, it bestows all accomplishments and treasures according to one's fitness.
That which was sung at Kollagiri and other places with the cries of the compassionate,
as well as the songs of the *samaya*, and that which was spoken by Geṣarāṇa, Rakṣa, and others.
"O Mummuṇi, the Kollaira has arrived!
O Kakkola, it is very crowded; compassion must be shown, for no Rolā is being played.
Malaaja is playing the Kunduru drum, but the Ḍiṇḍima is not being beaten there."
There, food is eaten with great relish and wine is drunk deeply;
O friend Kālindarī, there the drum is never allowed to cease its beating.
The four fragrant substances—kathura, sihlā, and camphor—are applied;
māla flowers serve as fuel, and there śāli rice is eaten.
While applying collyrium to her eyes, she does not notice the white plaster;
yet, when it is applied to her limbs, she perceives it there as if it were a fresh wound.

Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! O Hevajra, you who are the Indana-Jāhnavara bound to the tree of saṃsāra in divine form! You are that; therefore, hūṃ! Therefore, hūṃ! Therefore, you are that; therefore, you are that; you, you, hūṃ!
O Hevajra, you whose excellent feet are worshipped by the best of gods, whose garments are most pure and excellent—
*tuhaṃ* (you), *teṇa* (by that), *huṃ*, *te* (those), *te* (those), *huṃ*.
O Vajra, you who are packed with virtues, bow down, bow down! You have been struck by the excellence of the quality of immovable liberation.

First there is the smell of garlic, then again the smell of a vulture; thereafter follows the scent of camphor and sandalwood, characterized by the presiding presence of song. Following the end of the song, the cry of a swan and the hum of a bee are heard.

One should also perceive the sound of a jackal in the outer garden. Then, one should produce a sweet sound with the *nādya* of the Heruka mantra, agitated and whirling, accompanied by the clapping of hands (*haha-tāla*) and the beating of drums (*paṭaha*).
Khaṇḍi khaṇḍi, thuka thuka, thratha thratha, thrahotaṇḍi thrahotaṇḍi;
ta ḍhaṃ ta ḍhaṃ, drāka drāka, thuka thuka, tiṭiṃ tiṭiṃ, taṭava taṭava tāṃ.
Thus ends the instrumental music.

Therein, at the beginning of the drama, having touched the ground with a gesture of scattering a handful of flowers, one performs the *kamalāvarta* gesture through gestures such as salutation (*namaskāra*).
There should be as many mantra-seals (mantramudrās) as there are [deities] residing in the Śrī Heruka Tantra.
Thus, even while moving about amidst worldly activities, the yogin is called "one who possesses the power of the samaya-mudrās."
Moreover, it is stated in the *Ḍāka-bhāṣita* that the various inclinations of the mental continuum, such as passion for the Dharma and so forth, become the bringers of all specific qualities.
And so it is with the ketaka flower: once it has been consumed by a scent-elephant,
it certainly and completely transforms into musk.
For just as that which has been eaten by elephants passes away due to their lack of digestive power,
so too do passion and the other afflictions become purified for those who practice meditation.
Then Kolamaṇi, eating his meal— which was prepared to his heart's content and which caused the confusion of foot and non-foot through every visible sign— [proceeded].
Having perceived that means, may I, through this merit,
then bow with devotion and respectfully place the wheel upon my head.
One should always dwell with joy, as if one were wrapped in a shimmering garment.
By whatever merit has been acquired through this ritual of the *bali* wheel,
may the entire world always consist of great bliss.
The ritual procedure for the *bali* circle is completed.
